title: LGV Lemma 2×2: Lindström-Gessel-Viennot via Involution Bijection
description: Proves the 2×2 case of the Lindström-Gessel-Viennot (LGV) Lemma: the number of non-intersecting pairs of lattice paths equals the determinant of path count matrix. The crossing lemma is proved via column entry order analysis, and the Lindström involution provides a sign-reversing bijection between intersecting pairs. 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

overview.historicalContext: The Lindström-Gessel-Viennot (LGV) Lemma (Lindström 1973, Gessel-Viennot 1985) is a fundamental tool in combinatorics that counts non-intersecting lattice path systems using determinants. The 2×2 case states: given sources A₁, A₂ and targets B₁, B₂, the number of non-intersecting path pairs (A₁→B₁, A₂→B₂) equals e(A₁,B₁)·e(A₂,B₂) - e(A₁,B₂)·e(A₂,B₁), where e(A,B) is the number of monotone lattice paths from A to B. This file provides a complete formal proof with a novel crossing lemma via column entry order analysis.
overview.problemStatement: Prove the 2×2 LGV Lemma: for source points A₁=(0,a₁), A₂=(0,a₂) with a₁<a₂ and target points B₁=(m,b₁), B₂=(m,b₂) with b₁<b₂, the number of non-intersecting path pairs (P₁:A₁→B₁, P₂:A₂→B₂) equals C(m+b₁-a₁, m)·C(m+b₂-a₂, m) - C(m+b₂-a₁, m)·C(m+b₁-a₂, m).
overview.text: Lattice paths are encoded as lists of Booleans (false = East, true = North). The key function northBeforeEast l k counts North steps before the k-th East step, giving the y-coordinate when entering column k. The Crossing Lemma (fully proved) shows that if P₁ enters the grid lower than P₂ but exits higher, they must share a lattice point — proved by tracking column entry order via a disjoint interval monotonicity argument. The Lindström involution swaps path tails at the first shared point, creating a sign-reversing bijection on intersecting pairs. The LGV formula follows by inclusion-exclusion.
overview.proofStrategy: Part I defines LPath (Bool list), step counts, and PathMN (paths with exactly m East and n North steps). Path count is proved via binomial coefficients. Part II develops northBeforeEast and colEntry. Part III proves nonIntersecting_entry_order (the column entry preservation lemma) by induction on columns. Part IV proves the Crossing Lemma. Part V develops visitedPoints, sharedPoints, posAfter infrastructure. Part VI defines swapAtPoint and proves its involutivity and path structure preservation. Part VII defines the Lindström involution and proves it is a bijection on intersecting pairs. Part VIII assembles lgv_lemma_2x2 and derives ballot formula + Vandermonde identity.
keyInsights: northBeforeEast is the key invariant: it tracks the y-coordinate at column boundaries and is monotone in k
Crossing Lemma proof: use induction on columns — P₁ enters each column lower than P₂, so if P₁ ends higher, they must cross somewhere
disjoint interval argument: if paths are non-intersecting, their visited y-ranges in each column are disjoint (intervals don't overlap)
Lindström involution: swapping at the first crossing point gives an involution on intersecting pairs, proving the determinant formula
swapAtPoint involutivity: swapping twice recovers the original pair — proved by showing the new first crossing point equals the original
LGV formula follows: |NI pairs| = |all pairs| - |intersecting pairs| = e(A₁,B₁)e(A₂,B₂) - |involution pairs with wrong targets| = determinant

conclusion.summary: A complete, axiom-free formalization of the 2×2 LGV Lemma with a novel proof of the Crossing Lemma via column entry order analysis. The Lindström involution is fully constructed and proved to be a sign-reversing bijection on intersecting path pairs. 138 theorems, 0 axioms, 0 sorries across 2878 lines.
conclusion.implications: The LGV Lemma is a cornerstone of algebraic combinatorics, used in proofs of the hook-length formula, Schur polynomial identities, and determinantal point processes. This formalization provides Lean 4 infrastructure for lattice path arguments that can be extended to the general LGV lemma (arbitrary path systems) and to applications in representation theory.
